newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel opens Gaza road to Arabs closed two years.
newsitem.headline: Israel opens Gaza road to Arabs closed two years.

text.p: Israel allowed the reopening to Palestinians on Thursday of a Gaza Strip road closed two years ago, in a step a PLO police commander said reflected an improved atmosphere.
The road near the Jewish settlement of Netzarim had been closed to Palestinians since the killing of three soldiers by an Islamist suicide bomber on a bicycle in November 1994.

"It coincides with the general reconciliatory atmosphere," said Brigadier-General Saeb al-Ajez, Palestinian police commander in the northern strip, who took part in the reopening with an Israeli commander.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat met for the first time in 12 weeks on Tuesday at the Israeli-Gaza Strip border for a summit that both sides hailed as positive.

As the road was reopened, Palestinian and Israeli teams met in Jerusalem to hammer out a deal by next week that would give self-rule to Hebron, the last Palestinian town scheduled for autonomy in the West Bank.
The Netzarim road, two kms (1.2 miles) long, had been limited to use by the Israeli army, Jewish settlers and Palestinian police and dignitaries.
Ajez said that despite the official reopening, it would take some time before all Palestinians would be allowed to use it.
Six military jeeps -- three Israeli and three Palestinian -- travelled the road to officially reopen it. The military post where the three soldiers were killed has been moved to a site off the road.

The road has been a source of tension. Last month Israeli soldiers faced Palestinian motorists in a tense standoff on the road which has been patrolled jointly by Israeli and Palestinian forces over the last two years.
Jewish settlers on Wednesday laid a ceremonial cornerstone for what they said would be a new neighbourhood of Netzarim to protest at the reopening of the road to Palestinian traffic.

"Opening that road to Palestinians will endanger the settlement," Netzarim spokesman Shlomo Kostiner told Reuters on Wednesday. He said he envisaged 140 homes on the site, boosting Netzarim's population from 200 Jews to 1,000.
He said settlers had yet to receive building permits.

Israel turned over most of the Gaza Strip to Palestinian self-rule in mid-1994 but retained control of Jewish settlements there. Some 3,000 Jews live amid one million Palestinians in the impoverished territory.
The fate of the Jews in Gaza, Hebron and other West Bank settlements will be decided in "final-status" talks between Israel and the Palestinians due to be completed by May 1999.
